overview: GE Vernova was spun off from General Electric in April 2024 as a pure-play global energy company organized into three segments: Power (gas, nuclear, hydro and steam turbines plus long-term services), Wind (onshore, offshore and LM Wind Power blades), and Electrification (grid equipment, power conversion/storage, and electrification software). The company sells and services power generation and grid equipment to utilities, independent power producers, industrials, and increasingly hyperscale data-center developers, and is positioned as one of the primary beneficiaries of the AI-driven surge in electricity demand and global grid modernization.

business_model.summary: GE Vernova generates revenue from selling heavy capital equipment (gas turbines, nuclear/hydro/steam plant equipment, wind turbines, transformers and grid gear) combined with a large, high-margin, multi-decade services/aftermarket business (roughly 74% of the Power segment backlog is services). Equipment sales are lumpy and project-based with long lead times (multi-year order-to-revenue conversion, now including gas turbine slot reservations extending toward the end of the decade), while services revenue is recurring and provides a more stable, higher-margin annuity stream. The February 2026 acquisition of the remaining 50% of Prolec GE (a transformer joint venture with Mexico's Xignux) added a large, growing Electrification manufacturing business.

revenue_streams.name: Electrification (grid equipment, software, Prolec GE transformers)

business_model.customer_type: B2B - utilities, independent power producers, grid operators, industrial customers, and a fast-growing hyperscaler/data-center developer customer base (Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Oracle among reported counterparties)
business_model.geographic_mix: Global, with meaningful concentration in North America and Europe; Asia is a key growth region for gas turbines and nuclear SMR (BWRX-300) deployment; segment backlog approaching $176B (record) with a stated ambition to reach ~$200B total backlog by 2027

competitive_position.market_position: Top-3 global gas turbine OEM alongside Siemens Energy and Mitsubishi Power (together ~two-thirds of the gas turbine market for plants under construction); Mitsubishi Power led with ~35% of global MW orders in 2023 vs. Siemens Energy ~24% and GE ~16%, but GE Vernova dominates Asia's under-construction gas turbine market with ~38% share. In offshore/onshore wind, Vestas leads globally (~30% ex-China share) while Chinese OEMs Goldwind and Mingyang compete aggressively on price. GE Vernova/Hitachi's BWRX-300 is a leading Western small modular reactor (SMR) design, with the first unit under construction at Ontario Power Generation's Darlington site.

moat_factors.description: Massive global installed base of gas turbines and grid equipment creates a decades-long, high-margin services and parts revenue stream (Power segment backlog is 74% services) with high switching costs for utility customers.
Nuclear (BWRX-300) and large gas turbine manufacturing require extensive certification, safety approvals, and engineering expertise that create high barriers for new entrants.

Gas turbine and transformer manufacturing capacity is difficult to add quickly; GE Vernova's backlog visibility (100+ GW gas turbine backlog/slot reservations) gives it pricing power in a supply-constrained market.
Decades of GE engineering legacy in power generation lend credibility with utility and government customers on multi-billion-dollar, multi-decade projects.

weaknesses: Offshore wind has been a chronic loss-maker (~$0.3-0.4B in segment losses tied to Vineyard Wind and Dogger Bank project delays/contract disputes), with litigation risk (Vineyard Wind lawsuit)
Wind segment overall lags Power and Electrification in profitability and growth
Complex, still-maturing standalone financial and operating infrastructure less than two years post spin-off
Long equipment lead times mean current record bookings will not convert to revenue for years, creating execution and cost-inflation risk
Increasing reliance on a concentrated set of hyperscaler customers for incremental data-center-driven demand

growth_drivers: AI/data-center electricity demand driving unprecedented gas turbine and grid equipment orders — gas turbine backlog reached 100 GW in Q1 2026 (up from 83 GW at YE2025), targeting 110+ GW of combined backlog/slot reservations by year-end 2026

Electrification segment data-center equipment orders exceeded $5B year-to-date through Q1 2026, more than double all of 2025, driven by direct agreements with hyperscalers (Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Oracle reported as customers/counterparties)

Grid modernization and transmission buildout globally, further scaled by the February 2026 Prolec GE acquisition, which consolidated a leading transformer manufacturer into the Electrification segment
Nuclear renaissance: BWRX-300 SMR pipeline expanding via agreements/MOUs in Poland, Southeast Asia, and a gas-plus-nuclear power plant partnership (Blue Energy, Texas, August 2026)
Services/aftermarket monetization of a large global installed base providing high-margin, recurring cash flow to fund reinvestment
Record and growing total backlog (~$176B as of Q1 2026, targeting ~$200B by 2027) providing multi-year revenue visibility
Capital allocation shift to shareholder returns: doubled dividend, buyback authorization raised to $10B, while maintaining investment-grade balance sheet discipline

business.risk: Offshore wind losses and contract disputes
business.description: Vineyard Wind and Dogger Bank delays drove roughly $300-400M in wind segment losses; Vineyard Wind has sued GE Vernova over an alleged attempt to abandon its turbine supply contract.

business.risk: Customer/demand concentration in AI data centers
business.description: A large share of incremental order growth is tied to a small number of hyperscaler capex decisions, which could slow if AI infrastructure spending decelerates or is delayed.
Multi-year gas turbine and grid equipment backlogs must be executed profitably despite input cost inflation, tariffs, and supply chain constraints over several years.
Utilities and hyperscalers still lack common operating standards for grid interconnection, which could slow the pace at which backlog converts to installed, revenue-generating capacity.

financial.description: The Prolec GE acquisition added roughly $2.6B of new debt (total debt rose from ~$289M at FY2025 to ~$2.85B by Q1 2026), though management targets remaining below 1x net debt/adjusted EBITDA.

FY2025 net income included a ~$2.9B U.S. deferred tax valuation allowance release, and Q1 2026 net income included a ~$4.5B pre-tax non-cash M&A remeasurement gain from the Prolec GE step-acquisition — neither reflects ongoing operating earnings power, and investors must look through to operating income/EBITDA.

financial.risk: Working capital / cash conversion in long-cycle equipment business
financial.description: Progress billings and milestone payments on large multi-year projects can create working capital swings.

regulatory.description: BWRX-300 SMR deployments in Canada, Poland, and Southeast Asia depend on country-specific nuclear regulatory approvals that could delay timelines.
Tariffs have been cited as a specific drag on Wind segment profitability and could affect global equipment sourcing and manufacturing costs more broadly.
Government incentives (or their removal) for renewables, nuclear, and grid investment in the U.S. and EU could alter the pace of orders across segments.

macro.risk: Interest rate sensitivity of utility/IPP capex
macro.description: Customer capital spending on power generation and grid projects is sensitive to financing costs and could soften in a higher-for-longer rate environment.
A significant slowdown or pause in AI data-center buildout by hyperscalers would remove a key incremental demand driver behind the current gas turbine and electrification supercycle narrative.
Steel, copper, and other input costs affect equipment margins, particularly in Wind and Electrification manufacturing.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global power generation and grid equipment demand is in a multi-year upcycle driven by AI/data-center electrification, industrial reshoring, and grid modernization/decarbonization; gas turbine capacity is effectively sold out through the end of the decade at several major OEMs.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Historically cyclical (equipment orders tied to utility/IPP capex cycles), but currently supported by a structural demand step-change from AI power needs; large services backlog dampens cyclicality relative to a pure equipment maker.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — customer project financing costs affect order timing, though multi-year backlog provides revenue visibility largely insulated from near-term rate moves.

recent_developments.event: Raised FY2026 guidance again: revenue to $45.5-46.5B (from $44.5-45.5B) and free cash flow to $11.5-12.5B (from $6.5-7.5B); adjusted EBITDA margin guidance maintained at 12-14%.

Reported net income of $4.75B (50.9% net margin) driven by a ~$4.5B pre-tax non-cash M&A remeasurement gain on the Prolec GE step-acquisition; total orders up 88% organically to $24.2B, record backlog of $176B; gas turbine backlog reached 100 GW.

Completed acquisition of the remaining 50% of Prolec GE (transformer JV with Xignux) for $5.275B, funded roughly equally with cash and ~$2.6B of new debt; results now consolidated into the Electrification segment, immediately accretive to EBITDA before synergies.

Reported FY2025 net income of $4.9B (12.8% margin), which included a ~$2.9B U.S. deferred tax valuation allowance release reflecting improved outlook for sustained U.S. profitability; increased 2026 outlook alongside the Prolec GE deal announcement.
Board doubled the quarterly dividend to $0.50/share and raised share buyback authorization to $10B (from $6B) as part of a broader multi-year capital allocation update.

Continued offshore wind losses tied to Vineyard Wind and Dogger Bank; Vineyard Wind subsequently filed suit against GE Vernova alleging attempted contract abandonment; company reportedly weighing further offshore wind job cuts (~900 positions) to curb losses.

Expanded nuclear pipeline: BWRX-300 MOUs/agreements in Poland (generic design progress), Southeast Asia (with Hitachi), and a gas-plus-nuclear 2.5 GW power plant partnership with Blue Energy in Texas (August 2026).

Data-center-linked orders accelerated sharply: Electrification segment booked $2.4B in data-center equipment orders in a single quarter, more than all of 2025; total data-center orders exceeded $5B year-to-date through Q1 2026.

items.notes: Raised from prior $44.5-45.5B guidance given at Q1 2026, driven by record backlog and accelerating orders.
Sharply raised from prior $6.5-7.5B guidance, reflecting stronger operating cash generation and working capital dynamics including customer advances on long-cycle orders.
Unchanged despite revenue and FCF upgrades, implying margin expansion is not yet the primary driver of the raised outlook.
Backlog already at a record ~$176B as of Q1 2026 ($13B sequential increase), putting the 2027 target within reach ahead of schedule.
Up from 100 GW at Q1 2026 and 83 GW at YE2025, reflecting continued hyperscaler/data-center-driven demand.

items.target: At least one-third of cash generation returned to shareholders
items.notes: Supported by doubled dividend ($0.50/share quarterly) and buyback authorization increased to $10B from $6B; company states commitment to maintaining an investment-grade balance sheet alongside organic investment and targeted M&A.

guidance.management_commentary: Management has repeatedly framed 2026 as an inflection point, citing AI/data-center power demand as a structural (not cyclical) driver of gas turbine and grid equipment orders, while reiterating investment-grade balance sheet discipline even after taking on acquisition debt for Prolec GE. Management continues to caution that offshore wind remains a drag requiring a highly selective approach to new order intake.

bull_case: GE Vernova sits at the center of the AI/data-center electrification supercycle, with gas turbine capacity effectively sold out for years and a record ~$176B backlog on track to reach ~$200B by 2027

Electrification segment (grid equipment, transformers, software), newly scaled by the Prolec GE acquisition, has the strongest demand and pricing dynamics of the three segments and is compounding data-center-driven orders (>$5B YTD through Q1 2026)
Large, high-margin services/aftermarket annuity (74% of Power backlog) provides durable, recurring cash flow that funds reinvestment and shareholder returns while dampening cyclicality

Management has repeatedly raised FY2026 guidance (revenue and especially free cash flow), doubled the dividend, and expanded buyback authorization to $10B, signaling confidence and balance sheet strength even after Prolec GE debt
Emerging nuclear optionality via BWRX-300 SMR (Canada, Poland, Southeast Asia, U.S.) provides a long-duration growth call option in a global nuclear renaissance
bear_case: Reported net income is heavily distorted by one-off, non-operating items — a ~$2.9B FY2025 tax valuation allowance release and a ~$4.5B Q1 2026 non-cash Prolec GE remeasurement gain — masking a much smaller underlying operating income run-rate (~$180-650M/quarter), so headline EPS/net income multiples are not meaningful valuation anchors
Offshore wind remains a persistent loss-maker with active litigation (Vineyard Wind) and project delays (Dogger Bank), and further impairments or contract losses cannot be ruled out

Valuation already prices in a long, uninterrupted AI-driven capex supercycle — analyst price targets range enormously ($940-$1,450), reflecting genuine disagreement about whether current gas turbine demand is structural or a cyclical peak that could reverse if hyperscaler capex slows
Multi-year lead times mean today's record bookings will not convert to revenue and cash flow for years, exposing the company to input cost inflation, tariffs, and execution risk over that horizon

New acquisition debt (~$2.6B for Prolec GE) and rapidly growing balance sheet leverage, combined with capital-intensive nuclear and grid investments, add financial risk if the demand supercycle decelerates
